title: The Nanda Dynasty
description: An illustrated map of the rise of Magadha and its Nanda kings, from Bimbisara’s Rajagriha through the Nandas’ wealth and great army and Alexander’s halt at the Beas, to their fall to Chandragupta and Chanakya about 322 BCE.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of Magadha and the Nanda kingdom, from the 6th or 5th century to about 322 BCE
note: Based on Greek and Latin writers, Kharavela’s inscription, coins, and Puranic, Buddhist, Jain, Sri Lankan and Tamil traditions written down centuries later; each chapter says which it follows. The sources often disagree, and dates before 326 BCE are uncertain and debated. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: Magadha among the great kingdoms
steps.text: Magadha, in today’s south Bihar, is one of sixteen great kingdoms (mahajanapadas) named in Buddhist and Jain texts. Its first capital, Rajagriha, sits in a ring of five hills, guarded by stone walls whose remains still stand. Historians point to its fertile rice land, forests full of elephants and iron ore in the hills to the south.

steps.title: Bimbisara takes Anga
steps.text: Buddhist texts name Bimbisara, a patron of the Buddha, as the king who began Magadha’s rise. He conquers Anga to the east, with its river port of Champa on the Ganga, and makes marriage alliances with Kosala, the Lichchhavis of Vaishali and Madra. His dates, like the Buddha’s, are debated.

steps.title: Ajatashatru and the Vajjis
steps.text: Ajatashatru, who Buddhist tradition says seized the throne from his father, fights Kosala and then the Vajji confederacy across the Ganga, a league of clans ruled by assemblies at Vaishali. Jain texts say he won with two new war machines: a great stone-thrower and a chariot with swinging maces. After a long war, Vaishali falls to Magadha.

steps.title: A fort on the Ganga
steps.text: To face the Vajjis, Ajatashatru’s ministers fortify a village, Pataligrama, where the Son river meets the Ganga. A Buddhist text says the Buddha passed by and foretold a great city, threatened only by fire, flood and quarrels. Jain and Puranic tradition say Ajatashatru’s son Udayin later made it Magadha’s capital.

steps.title: Shishunaga defeats Avanti
steps.text: Sri Lankan chronicles say the people of Magadha, tired of kings who killed their fathers, set aside Bimbisara’s line and made a minister, Shishunaga, king. The Puranas say he broke the power of Avanti, Magadha’s great rival in the west, ruled from Ujjain. Kosala and Vatsa also pass to Magadha, though exactly when is uncertain.

steps.title: The council at Vaishali
steps.text: Sri Lankan chronicles say that about a hundred years after the Buddha’s death, in the reign of Kalashoka, son of Shishunaga, monks gather at Vaishali to settle a quarrel over the rules, such as whether monks may accept gold and silver. It is remembered as the Second Buddhist Council. Kalashoka may be the king the Puranas call Kakavarna.

steps.title: A barber’s son?
steps.text: The Nandas’ rise is told in different ways. The Roman writer Curtius says the reigning king’s father was a barber who became the queen’s lover, murdered the old king and his sons. Jain tradition also calls the first Nanda a barber’s son. The poet Bana tells of a Shishunaga king, Kakavarna, stabbed in the throat near his city.

steps.title: Mahapadma, sole ruler
steps.text: The Puranas name the first Nanda Mahapadma, son of the last Shishunaga king by a Shudra mother. They call him sole ruler (ekarat), destroyer of all the old warrior (kshatriya) lines, who brought the earth under one umbrella. They give him 88 years and his eight sons twelve more. Sri Lankan chronicles instead count nine brothers ruling 22 years.

steps.title: The Nandas in Kalinga
steps.when: 4th century BCE, recalled two or three centuries later
steps.text: Two or three centuries later, Kharavela, king of Kalinga, has his deeds carved above a cave at Udayagiri. The inscription names a Nanda king (Nandaraja) twice: for a canal he opened in Kalinga, and for a Jain image (Kalinga Jina) he carried off, which Kharavela proudly brings home. So the Nandas probably ruled Kalinga.
steps.today: Today: the Hathigumpha cave, Udayagiri, near Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

steps.title: An army the Greeks feared
steps.text: Greek and Latin writers describe the king of the Prasii (from prachya, ‘easterners’) and the Gangaridai, whom they call Agrammes or Xandrames. Curtius gives him 200,000 foot soldiers, 20,000 horsemen, 2,000 chariots and 3,000 elephants; Plutarch says 8,000 chariots and 6,000 elephants. The numbers may be exaggerated, but they echo Indian memories of Nanda might.

steps.title: The Nanda treasure
steps.text: The last Nanda is remembered as Dhana Nanda, ‘Nanda of wealth’. A Sri Lankan commentary says he taxed even skins, gums, trees and stones, and hid a vast hoard in a rock under the Ganga. Far to the south, the Tamil poet Mamulanar recalls the wealth of the Nandas, gathered at Pataliputra and hidden in the Ganga’s floods.

steps.title: Ministers and magic
steps.when: told from the early centuries CE to the 11th
steps.text: Later stories fill the Nanda court with clever ministers. Jain tradition names Shakatala, minister of the last Nanda, whose son Sthulabhadra became a leading Jain monk. The 11th-century Kathasaritsagara tells of the grammarian Vararuchi, and of a man who entered a dead Nanda king’s body by magic and ruled as ‘Yogananda’. None of it can be checked.

steps.title: Alexander crosses the Indus
steps.text: In 326 BCE Alexander of Macedon crosses the Indus into the Punjab. Ambhi, king of Taxila, welcomes him, and at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) Alexander defeats King Porus in a hard battle against war elephants, then keeps him as an ally. He marches east, towards the Ganga plain and the Nanda kingdom.
steps.today: Today: the Jhelum river, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: Turned back at the Beas
steps.text: At the Hyphasis (Beas) a local king, Phegeus, tells Alexander of the mighty king on the Ganga. His soldiers, worn out by years of marching and weeks of monsoon rain, refuse to go on; his officer Coenus speaks for them. Alexander raises twelve altars and turns back. How much the Nanda army’s fame mattered is debated.
steps.today: Today: the Beas river, Punjab, India.

steps.title: A young man meets Alexander
steps.text: Plutarch writes that the young Chandragupta, Sandrokottos to the Greeks, saw Alexander, and later said Alexander could easily have taken the east, because its king was hated for his wickedness and low birth. The Roman historian Justin says Sandrokottos offended Alexander with his boldness and escaped being killed. Where they met is not recorded.
steps.today: Today: Taxila’s ruins are a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Chanakya’s vow
steps.text: In tradition, Chanakya, a Brahmin scholar, perhaps from Taxila, is insulted at Dhana Nanda’s court: in a Buddhist version he is thrown out of the seat of honour in the king’s alms hall. He vows to destroy the Nandas, and later tellings say he left his topknot (shikha) untied until he did. He finds Chandragupta to lead the fight.

steps.title: Start from the edges
steps.text: Buddhist and Jain stories say a first attack on the heart of Magadha failed. In hiding, the pair heard a mother scold her child for burning his fingers in the middle of a dish of hot food: eat from the cool edges first. So they took the borderlands first. Justin says Sandrokottos drove out Alexander’s governors once Alexander died.

steps.title: The fall of the Nandas
steps.text: About 322 BCE Chandragupta and Chanakya take Pataliputra. The Buddhist Milindapanha recalls a vast battle against Bhaddasala, the Nanda general. Jain tradition says the defeated king was allowed to leave with what one chariot could carry, and his daughter chose to go with Chandragupta. Other tellings say Dhana Nanda was killed. Either way, the Maurya age begins.

steps.title: Rakshasa’s loyalty
steps.when: a play of perhaps the 4th to 8th century CE
steps.text: The play Mudrarakshasa (Rakshasa’s Signet Ring), by Vishakhadatta, imagines what came next. Rakshasa, the last Nanda’s loyal minister, plots to restore his master’s line. Chanakya outwits him with Rakshasa’s own signet ring and a forged letter, then wins him over to serve Chandragupta. Its date is debated, and it is drama, not history.
steps.today: Today: still performed and studied in India.

steps.title: Coins without names
steps.text: Magadha’s silver coins (karshapana) were bent bars and flat pieces stamped with symbols such as suns, wheels, animals and hills, but no names or dates. Hoards show these coins spreading across north India as Magadha grew. Experts sort them into series and suggest which belong to the Nanda years, but no coin can be tied to a named king.
steps.today: Today: hoards are held in museums across India.

steps.title: What the Mauryas inherited
steps.text: The Nandas ruled for a short time, perhaps a few decades, but they joined most of the Ganga plain under one king, with a standing army, a full treasury and a tax system. Chandragupta took over that machine and built the first empire to cover most of the subcontinent. Their capital now lies beneath modern Patna.
steps.today: Today: Patna, capital of Bihar, India.

items.name: Bimbisara
items.text: Buddhist texts make Bimbisara a friend and patron of the Buddha, who gave the young order a park near Rajagriha. He built Magadha’s power by conquest, taking Anga, and by marriage. Buddhist tradition says his son Ajatashatru imprisoned him and he died in prison. Jain tradition knows him as Shrenika.

items.name: Ajatashatru
items.text: Son of Bimbisara, called Kunika in Jain texts. Buddhist tradition says he seized the throne, later regretted his father’s death and turned to the Buddha, and that the First Buddhist Council met at Rajagriha in his reign. He defeated Kosala and the Vajjis, and fortified Pataligrama on the Ganga.

items.name: Shishunaga
items.role: King of Magadha, founder of a dynasty
items.text: A minister made king, Sri Lankan chronicles say, when the people set aside Bimbisara’s line. The Puranas say he broke the power of Avanti. His son, Kalashoka, may be the Kakavarna of the Puranas; the Second Buddhist Council met at Vaishali in his reign. Indian and Sri Lankan lists of these kings do not agree.

items.name: Mahapadma Nanda
items.role: Founder of the Nanda dynasty, in the Puranas
items.text: The Puranas name Mahapadma as the first Nanda, son of a Shudra mother, and the first sole ruler (ekarat) of the north, who ended the old warrior lines. Jain tradition calls the first Nanda a barber’s son. Curtius’s barber-king, father of the reigning king, may be him. A later Buddhist list instead begins the nine Nandas with Ugrasena.

items.name: Kharavela
items.life: about the 1st century BCE; dates debated
items.text: A Jain king of Kalinga whose long inscription at the Hathigumpha cave, Udayagiri, records his reign year by year: wars, festivals and buildings. It is one of the few early sources to name a Nanda king, and so one of the best clues that the Nandas ruled Kalinga.

items.name: Dhana Nanda
items.role: Last Nanda king, in later sources
items.text: The last Nanda is named Dhana Nanda only in later Buddhist sources; Greek and Latin writers call the king of their day Agrammes or Xandrames, perhaps the same man. Tradition remembers him as rich, greedy and unpopular. He was overthrown by Chandragupta and Chanakya; whether he was killed or sent away, the stories disagree.

items.name: Mamulanar
items.life: Not known; a poet of the Sangam age
items.text: A poet of the early Tamil Sangam anthologies. In a poem of the Akananuru he mentions the wealth of the Nandas, gathered at Pataliputra and hidden in the Ganga’s floods. That a poet so far south knew the story shows how famous the Nanda treasure was. He also mentions the Mauryas.

items.name: Alexander of Macedon
items.role: King of Macedon, conqueror of the Persian Empire
items.text: After conquering the Persian Empire, Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush and the Indus in 327 to 326 BCE. He beat Porus at the Hydaspes, but at the Beas his army refused to march on towards the Ganga and the Nanda kingdom. He turned back down the Indus and died at Babylon in 323 BCE.

items.name: Porus
items.role: King between the Jhelum and the Chenab
items.text: Porus, perhaps Puru or Paurava in Indian languages, faced Alexander at the Hydaspes with war elephants and lost. Greek writers say that, asked how he wished to be treated, he answered ‘like a king’. Alexander kept him as ruler and ally. His Indian name and family are not recorded in Indian sources.

items.name: Coenus
items.text: A Macedonian commander who had fought in all of Alexander’s great battles. At the Beas, Arrian says, he spoke for the exhausted army, telling Alexander the men longed to see their homes again. Alexander gave way. Coenus died of illness soon afterwards, back at the Hydaspes.

items.name: Chanakya
items.role: Brahmin teacher and minister, in tradition
items.text: Also called Kautilya and Vishnugupta. Indian, Buddhist and Jain traditions all make him the mind behind Chandragupta, who swore to destroy the Nandas after being insulted at their court. Tradition credits him with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft; scholars think it was written or revised later. Greek writers never mention him.

items.name: Chandragupta Maurya
items.text: His origins are uncertain: Buddhist texts make him a Moriya of warrior rank, some later works call him low-born. Greek writers name him Sandrokottos. With Chanakya he drove out Alexander’s governors and overthrew the Nandas, taking their army and treasury, then built an empire from Afghanistan to Bengal.

items.name: Rakshasa
items.role: Minister of the last Nanda, in Mudrarakshasa
items.text: In Vishakhadatta’s play, Rakshasa is the last Nanda’s chief minister, so loyal that he keeps plotting after his master’s fall. Chanakya admires that loyalty and wants it for Chandragupta. The play ends with Rakshasa, outwitted, agreeing to serve the new king. No other source mentions him.
